name: Electron speed
seoTitle: Electron speed Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Electron speed: work out accelerating potential from the velocity difference. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Electron speed calculator is a free, no-sign-up physics tool. Fill in the 1 field it asks for and it works out accelerating potential straight away, with the formula shown underneath. It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Electron speed calculator work?
sections.html:
The Electron speed calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports accelerating potential in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the velocity difference.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilometers per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Electron speed calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Accelerating potential=(227734589 ÷ 80108831000000000000) × (classical velocity ^ 2)
Relativistic velocity=299792458 × the square root of (1 − (Temperature 1 ^ 2))
Accelerating potential=(40935528884500 ÷ 80108831) × (1 − Temperature 1) ÷ temp1
Relativistic velocity=velocity difference + classical velocity

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per second
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per second
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per second

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Electron speed calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the velocity difference — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Electron speed calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — velocity difference for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the Electron speed calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns accelerating potential, derived from the velocity difference. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Electron speed calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the velocity difference, which is 1 field in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter accelerating potential in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Accelerating potential opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Electron speed calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
